content.intro: This lesson covers Understanding Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock. It sits in Module 11, Modules, Crates, Packages, and Cargo, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock matters when you work with reproducible project and team workflows. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Rust tooling makes the build, dependency graph, formatting, linting, and test steps repeatable. Use the project’s declared toolchain and Cargo metadata rather than relying on undocumented local state.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Understanding Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Cargo.toml declares a package and dependency intent; Cargo.lock records a resolved graph for reproducible application builds. Keep module visibility deliberate.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Understanding Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
